clue.text: Pie's top — it's mashed veg

indicators.note: mashed vegetables are pulped and broken up, so these words' letters are crushed into a new order

parts.note: the possessive S counts here as a letter of the fodder
the apostrophe is ignored and its three letters are kept

explanation.surface: Someone describes a pie crust made of mashed vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mashed' rearranges PIESTOPITS, the letters of 'Pie's top it's', into the French name for small garden peas.
explanation.definitionFit: Petits pois are small green peas, a vegetable, so 'veg' covers them as an example.

clue.text: Pole in paid employment

explanation.surface: A Polish worker has a salaried job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person, but it means an upright stake.
explanation.definitionFit: A post is an upright stake fixed in the ground, and also a job or appointment.

clue.text: Story told by dog

indicators.note: a story told is spoken out, so the word for it is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a story is a tale

explanation.surface: A tale is narrated by a canine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog' looks like a noun for the narrator, but it is the verb meaning to follow someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to shadow or follow them closely, which is what dogging them means.

clue.text: A little bit dry in relation to gossip…

annotationWithheld.why: A little bit dry in relation to gossip (6-6): TITTLE is 'A little bit' and 'gossip' the definition, but no reading of 'dry in relation to' gives TATTLE without a word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: A little bit dry in relation to gossip…

clue.text: …that's left Bishop feeling honoured

indicators.note: something that has left has gone away, so these letters are dropped from the name

parts.note: Bishop Proudie is the bishop in Trollope's Barchester novels
i.e. is short for id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: Gossip that a bishop has heard leaves him flattered.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop Proudie is a character in Anthony Trollope's Barchester novels; dropping IE ('that's') leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be proud of something is to feel honoured and pleased by it.

clue.text: Nitrate, in solution, is liable to move around

indicators.note: a solution is a mixture that dissolves something, so the letters are dissolved and remixed

explanation.surface: A chemical dissolved in liquid tends to circulate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in solution' looks like a chemistry phrase, but 'in' is part of the fodder and 'solution' rearranges NITRATEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Itinerant describes someone travelling from place to place, such as a wandering worker.

clue.text: Entrance to building from the back looks out to sea

indicators.note: taking each word from its back end means picking the final letter of every word that follows

explanation.surface: A house's rear entrance faces the open sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the back' seems to place the entrance at the rear of the building, but it picks the last letter of each of 'looks out to sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is a Greek covered colonnade or portico, the pillared approach at the front of a classical building.

clue.text: In vehicle overturning abroad, I get on to railway track

indicators.note: in places the foreign word for I inside the turned-over vehicle
overturning means the word for the vehicle is turned end to end

parts.note: a cart is a simple vehicle
je is French for I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A foreign traveller describes climbing on board a train after a carriage tips over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturning' turns CART into TRAC, and JE (French 'I') goes inside it; 'get on' is a link word before TO and RY.
explanation.definitionFit: A trajectory is the path or course followed by a moving object, its track through space.

clue.text: Thus plentifully supplied, Reds could be understandably confused

indicators.note: confused means the letters of the long word are jumbled, and they contain the other word's letters too

explanation.surface: Communists given too much are naturally bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: Composite anagram: the answer plus REDS, shuffled, gives UNDERSTANDABLY ('confused').
explanation.definitionFit: Abundantly means in great quantity, the same as plentifully.

clue.text: King on the Mississippi

parts.note: a French monarch who was canonised gives his name to a big city on the banks of America's great river

explanation.surface: A monarch travels along the Mississippi river.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis IX of France was made a saint, and the Missouri city named after him stands on the Mississippi.
explanation.definitionFit: The canonised French monarch Louis IX shares his title with the Missouri river city founded by French traders.

clue.text: Forbidden to start a business centre

indicators.note: the centre of the whole phrase 'to start a business' is taken, its four middle letters

explanation.surface: Someone is banned from setting up a business hub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre' looks like part of 'business centre', but it takes the middle four of the sixteen letters of 'to start a business'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabu is an old spelling of taboo, meaning prohibited by custom or rule.

clue.text: Both sides have, opposing: players with a bit of wood — bats

parts.note: in cricket the two halves of the field are the off side and the on side
in cricket the two halves of the field are the off side and the on side
in bridge East and South sit as opponents, giving E and S
a chump is a short thick lump of wood

explanation.surface: Two teams of cricketers face each other with bats.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the field divides into the off side and the on side. 'bats' looks like cricket bats, but it means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Off one's chump is British slang for crazy, the same as being bats.

clue.text: Flourished peculiar weapon in battle

parts.note: fl. is the abbreviation of floruit, Latin for 'flourished', used in dates of historical figures
peculiar means odd
the Enfield is a British army rifle, named after the town where it was made

explanation.surface: Someone brandished a strange weapon during a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: FLODDEN FIELD was the 1513 battle in Northumberland where the English defeated the Scots and James IV died.
explanation.definitionFit: Flodden Field is the site and name of a famous Anglo-Scottish battle of 1513.

clue.text: Being hare-brained, start to show spite

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, taken here from 'show'

parts.note: cattiness is spiteful, malicious behaviour

explanation.surface: Someone behaving foolishly begins to act spitefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to show' reads as 'begin to display' but gives S, the first letter of 'show'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scattiness is flightiness or absent-mindedness, the state of being harebrained.

clue.text: It's undemanding, so ref's left out

indicators.note: out here means out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped and the four letters kept

explanation.surface: The match is easy because the referee has gone home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SOREFSLEFT, the letters of 'so ref's left'.
explanation.definitionFit: Effortless means easy, needing no strain, so it is undemanding.

clue.text: Composer's first song about to entertain restaurant

indicators.note: the first letter of the word Composer's is taken on its own
about here means surrounding, so the song's letters go around the other piece

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
to fete someone is to entertain them lavishly

explanation.surface: A composer's opening number is about to be played to diners at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to entertain' reads as 'ready to perform', but 'about' wraps ARIA round FETE, giving AFETERIA after the C.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafeteria is a self-service eating place, a kind of informal restaurant.

clue.text: Having ruined it, you would say "Goodness!"

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken, and the sound gives the answer

parts.note: 'Having ruined it, you would' becomes the spoken words 'wrecked it, you'd'

explanation.surface: After breaking something, a person exclaims in dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goodness!' looks like an exclamation of dismay, but it means moral virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectitude is moral uprightness, virtue or goodness of character.

clue.text: Lose head in temper time and again

indicators.note: losing its head means the word for temper drops its first letter

parts.note: to temper something is to soften it, moderate it

explanation.surface: Someone repeatedly flies into a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose head in temper' reads as losing one's cool, but it removes the S from SOFTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means frequently, happening repeatedly.

clue.text: Old woman can be seen by all embraced by a revolutionary

indicators.note: something embraced by another is held inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a Trot is short for a Trotskyist, a left-wing revolutionary
U is the British film certificate for 'universal', meaning suitable for everyone to see

explanation.surface: An elderly lady, visible to everyone, is hugged by a radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old trout' is British slang for a grumpy older woman. U is the British 'universal' film rating.
explanation.definitionFit: An 'old trout' is a disparaging informal term for an elderly woman, so the fish name stands for her.

clue.text: Church pet, a Tom, with fat back

parts.note: a cat is a common household pet
a tom is a male animal, so 'a Tom' is a he

indicators.note: back means the word for fat is read from end to start

parts.note: lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: A church pet, a tomcat, is plump around the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a Tom' looks like a cat's name, but it gives HE, a male. 'back' turns LARD into DRAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral is the principal church of a diocese, seat of a bishop.

clue.text: Electing Neil makes sense

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made into something new, so 'makes' signals a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Voting for someone named Neil is the sensible thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' rearranges the letters of 'Electing Neil'; 'makes sense' looks like one phrase, but 'sense' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Intelligence means good judgement or understanding, which is what having sense is.

clue.text: Fellow's catamaran finally sunk in lake

indicators.note: a thing sunk in a lake goes inside it, so a letter goes within the lake's name

parts.note: Lake Erie is one of North America's Great Lakes

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word catamaran

explanation.surface: A man's boat has gone down in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sunk in' puts N, the last letter of 'catamaran', inside ERIE. 'Fellow's' is 'Fellow is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie is a man's name, standing for any male person.

clue.text: Emperor given to looking both ways

indicators.note: looking both ways means the name reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A ruler is cautious, checking left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: Otto was the name of several Holy Roman Emperors; the name is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto I and other Holy Roman Emperors bore the name, so it names an emperor.

clue.text: Raise the river bank, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it signals that the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: a levee is an embankment along a river

explanation.surface: Someone proposes building up the riverside embankment.
explanation.walkthrough: A levee is a raised bank against river floods.
explanation.definitionFit: To levy is to raise a tax or troops, collecting them by authority.

clue.text: Ogled, I would say

indicators.note: say signals that the shortened form of the words is heard, not written

parts.note: I would contracts to I'd

explanation.surface: Someone admits they would have stared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' signals that I'D, short for 'I would', is pronounced like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to look at someone hard, so ogled and looked over are the same.

clue.text: Stand on one's head and spell 'dove'

parts.note: a spell is a turn or shift at doing something
a turtle is a turtle dove, a bird of the dove family

explanation.surface: A child is told to do a headstand and then spell out a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' looks like spelling a word, but it is a stint of duty.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn turtle is to capsize or flip upside down, standing on one's head in a figurative sense.

clue.text: Appeal for help round fair

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal asking for help
a round shape is an O

explanation.surface: A call for help comes from the fairground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round fair' suggests a fairground ride, but 'fair' means middling.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means average or passable, the same sense as fair in 'a fair performance'.

clue.text: Dictatorial father to politician of the right

parts.note: pere is French for father
MP is a Member of Parliament
a Tory is a British Conservative, a right-wing party member

explanation.surface: A dad is bossy towards a right-wing politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Peremptory means commanding and allowing no refusal, as a dictator would be.
